items.title: Increasing pay for lower wage workers
items.summary:
From 2014 to 2024, the share of U.S. hourly workers paid below $15 in real terms fell by two-thirds, from 38 percent to 13 percent. Why? We first distinguish the entry and exit of employers—wherein high-paying employers have supplanted low-paying ones—from organizational changes among incumbent employers. Organizational changes can be imposed on employers by external constraints, like labor market tightness, or emerge from the pursuit of new opportunities. Using panel data drawn from administrative records and job reviews, we bring this framework to bear on the recent wage gains at the bottom of the labor market. Contrary to predictions of creative destruction, we can trace only a small amount of these wage gains to the disappearance of low-wage organizations. Instead, the main driver of rising pay was low- and middle-paying incumbent employers of low-wage occupations increasing pay. These gains in low-wage occupations were associated with tightening labor markets and increased minimum wages. But over and above these external constraints, employers also pursued new opportunities for reorganizing work in low-skill jobs. Notwithstanding organizational inertia, major gains for workers’ pay can come from changes in existing workplaces.

That is from recent research by Clem Aeppli, Soohyun Roh, and Nathan Wilmers. Via the excellent Kevin Lewis .

items.title: Danish daughters
items.summary:
Using Danish administrative data, we compare parents of only children who experience a stroke at the same age and differ only in the gender of their child.

Before the stroke, parents of daughters and parents of sons follow similar health trajectories, with comparable levels of pre-existing conditions and healthcare utilization. After the stroke, a survival gap opens and grows, and parents of daughters are 1.5 percentage points more likely to be alive by year five. Over the same period, daughters adjust more than sons along several margins: they become more likely to live near their parents, less likely to be married, and have fewer children, consistent with greater involvement in informal caregiving.

Crucially, parents of daughters use more physical rehabilitation, an elective type of formal care that requires sustained engagement. Rather than crowding out formal provision, daughters appear more likely to help parents navigate and use professional services. Informal and formal care can therefore operate, at least in part, as complements in the response to severe health shocks.

That recent work is from recent work by Elin Colmsjö , Francesco Ruggieri, and Matteo Saccarola.  Via the excellent Samir Varma .

The post Danish daughters appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Will AI Growth Reach the Developing World?
items.summary:
Here is the abstract from a new NBER paper by Daniel Björkegren , David Lagakos & Mitchell VanVuren : 

This paper explores how economic growth driven by AI will impact the developing world. Our analysis is based on a growth model of a developed and developing economy where AI services are traded on the world market, and may substitute for or complement different labor inputs in production. Preferences allow for the possibility that demand for services provided by AI has an upper bound. The model predicts that developing countries may not benefit as much from AI-driven growth. First, they may lack complementary skills needed to fully utilize AI domestically. Second, they may be priced out of world markets due to their relatively lower productivity. We use our model to simulate how growth and welfare are affected by making workers more complementary to AI, subsidizing compute, speeding technology diffusion, and providing cash transfers. Numerical simulations of the model suggest that the potential for developing countries to be left behind – or having some workers lose in absolute terms – is substantial enough that researchers should study the impacts of AI on developing countries in real time.

I am more optimistic than the authors.  For one thing, in their model AI improves the productivity of legal services in say Africa, but not food.  That mix seems unlikely to me.  AI already makes rainfall prediction and crop management more productive, and it might over time help create more “miracle crops.”  A few other points:

items.title: *The Great Enrichment*
items.summary:
The author is my colleague Vincent Geloso and the subtitle is A New History of American Growth and Inequality, 1865-1945 .  Here is an excerpt from the very beginning:

…regardless of what improvements you think occurred during the Gilded Age and the Progressive Era, you are underestimating how much improvement there truly was.  From 1870 to the start off World War I, America experienced the fastest and most stunning rise in the quality of life of the downtrodden, the poor, the unskilled, the midskilled, and the average Joe (i.e., the poorest 90% of Americans) ever seen in human history up to that point.  Second, it was the period from World War I to the end of World War II that was marked by slower — though still substantial — gains for people at the bottom of the income ladder.  Third, the improvements in the living standards of the poorest 90 percent of the population were faster than those of the top 10 percent and as fast as those of the top 1 percent from 1870 to 191.  During those four decades, America was a lean and mean egalitarian growth machine .  Fourth, this machine was fueled by America’s exceptionally dynamic market economy, which allowed people to move to pursue better opportunities (either in terms of industries or in terms of geography).  While some state actions did contribute to this machine, market forces own the lion’s share, and, in many cases, they actually made government actions more effective.  Fifth, America developed a welfare state only because, in the aftermath of World War I, the growth machine slowed down.

items.title: Phonics-based Instruction and Student Achievement
items.summary:
That is a new NBER working paper by Alex Hollingsworth , Alberto Ortega & Nikolaos Zirogiannis .  Abstract:

Reading is a foundational skill, yet fewer than one in three US fourth graders read at a proficient level. How best to teach reading and improve educational attainment has been an active policy debate for decades. Recently, phonics-based approaches have surged in popularity, even though the largest attempt to put similar methods into classrooms was previously abandoned out of concerns that the program was ineffective. This paper studies Reading First, a nearly $1 billion per year federal program established under No Child Left Behind that promoted phonics-based instruction in K-3 classrooms. Exploiting administrative data from Texas and program eligibility formulas, we estimate effects via difference-in-differences and instrumental variables specifications. We find that eligibility increased third-grade reading test scores by 0.1 standard deviations and that effects persisted through at least the eighth grade. An analysis of digitized exam questions shows that treated students outperformed peers on questions that required basic decoding skills and those with more words, a benefit that also drove improvements in math scores. We follow exposed cohorts into early adulthood, finding that the program increased on-time high school graduation, college enrollment, four-year college completion, and adult earnings at age 25.

As with many “ban cell phones in schools” papers, I find these results underwhelming.  Nonetheless phonics education always has made sense to me.

items.title: AIs vs. humans in economics papers
items.summary:
Is agentic research any good? Dr Yanagizawa-Drott and his colleague, Olaf Willner, used an AI verifier to check 1,000 APE papers. None was error-free; 842 contained at least one severe error, including ones invalidating headline results. To see roughly how Ape stacks up against human primates, The Economist teamed up with Refine, the research-verification firm founded by Dr Golub. Refine chose 100 papers at random from those accepted for publication in the top five journals (including QJE and JPE ) in the first nine months of 2026. It then subjected them to thorough review using several frontier AI models plus a once-over for serious errors by a human reviewer. The exercise flagged 4,158 issues in the 100 papers. One in ten papers contained at least one grave error (other problems concerned interpretation or inconsistencies between tables and text).

The two exercises are not directly comparable, but human economists’ lower error rate might give them some hope. In ideas, too, people retain the edge. One experiment, by Alexis Akira Toda of Emory University, found that when considering papers on economic theory alone, AI lowers the cost of checking for a candidate flaw but “does not yet reliably substitute for the human judgment that locates the flaw in the first place”. Another, which compared APE papers with published papers found the difference is mostly in ideas, not execution. In a further study, Michele Zampa of the Geneva Graduate Institute used an AI referee to grade 981 AI papers and 41 human ones on things like the novelty of research questions and acknowledgment…
items.t: AIs vs. humans in economics papers

items.title: The Anthropic IPO
items.summary:
In general I am bullish on the commercial prospects of AI companies, including Anthropic (do note I am on the Advisory Board, though with zero governance role and zero access to internal information).

But I view today’s IPO as a sign of bearishness on any kind of extreme superintelligence, no matter what involved parties might say.

If superintelligence is coming soon, why turn yourself into a public company, with all the extra scrutiny and regulation that requires?  Raising extra money through debt is the obvious alternative — why cut other in on such an amazing deal?

Furthermore, true superintelligence is likely to raise real interest rates, which raises the return to borrowing today (you can always reinvest at higher rates later, if you do not need the money for compute, etc.).

Now raising money through debt would be relatively costly for Anthropic, but at the very least they could have shrunk the size of the IPO and borrowed more at the margin.  Claude says they would have had to pay about ten to eleven percent on that debt .  Alternately, they could just take on Jane Street, Citadel, and others and try to earn money through direct commercial activities (but in fact they cannot, note that).

So presumably Anthropic thinks that pending advances, whatever you might wish to call them, will not with any great certainty yield ten to eleven percent at the margin.  That is a perfectly fine view for them to hold, but you all should use the implied inference to calm down a bit about what is coming.

I myself am taking that wise and prudent financial decision under…
